text:
Predicates:
SpillsFoodClothing(x) ::: x spills a lot of food on his clothing.
NotablyTidy(x) ::: x is notably tidy.
ClumsyFoodie(x) ::: x is a clumsy foodie.
GoesOutFrequent(x) ::: x goes out frequently to find new food restaurants.
FoodRestaurant(x) ::: x is a food restaurant.
Cleanly(x) ::: x is cleanly.
ValuOrderSpotless(x) ::: x values order and spotlessness.
FamilyPrioritizeOrderSpotlessness(x) ::: x's family prioritizes order and spotlessness.
Peter ::: Peter.
Premises:
∀x (SpillsFoodClothing(x) → ¬NotablyTidy(x)) ::: If people spill a lot of food on their clothing, then they are not notably tidy.
∀x (ClumsyFoodie(x) ∧ GoesOutFrequent(x) → SpillsFoodClothing(x)) ::: All clumsy foodies who go out frequently are people who spill a lot of food on their clothing.
∀x (Cleanly(x) → NotablyTidy(x)) ::: If people are cleanly, then they are notably tidy.
∀x (ValuOrderSpotless(x) → Cleanly(x)) ::: If people value order and spotlessness, then they are cleanly.
∀x (FamilyPrioritizeOrderSpotlessness(x) → ValuOrderSpotless(x)) ::: All people whose families prioritize order and spotlessness themselves value order and spotlessness.
PeterIsClumsyFoodieGoesOutOrFamilyPrioritizesOrderSpotlessness ::: (ClumsyFoodie(Peter) ∧ GoesOutFrequent(Peter)) ∨ FamilyPrioritizeOrderSpotlessness(Peter)
Conclusion:
(PeterIsClumsyFoodieGoesOutOrFamilyPrioritizesOrderSpotlessness) ::: Peter is either a clumsy foodie who goes out frequently to find new food restaurants to try or someone whose family prioritizes order and spotlessness
